chunks: "I'd work in order of effectiveness. The first fix is technique: take off the long alligator clip.
Use a spring ground tip or just the probe barrel pressed against a ground point, the tip-and-barrel method.
That alone cuts the lead from roughly 150 nanohenries to about 10, and the loop area by a lot.

The second is to pick the ground point carefully: the nearest quiet ground, ideally a pad a couple of millimetres from the signal and connected to the plane with vias, not the power ground of a switching stage.
That's why I put ground pads next to test points when I design the board.
The third is better hardware: an active or low-capacitance probe with a short ground accessory, a soldered-in probe lead, or an SMA or MMCX connector on the board so a coax gives a controlled return.
For differential or floating signals I use a differential probe, which isn't referenced to scope ground.
For mains-type loops, I connect grounds at one point, power the DUT from an isolated or battery supply, or use a differential or isolated probe, and I never lift the scope's safety earth.
Last, I verify: short the tip to its ground at the pad and check the noise floor; shorten the loop further and see if the waveform changes.
When it stops changing, the loop is small enough."
